questions.q: What are the three criteria this lesson gives for picking a good capstone problem?
options: It must be naturally binary/quadratic in structure, small enough to brute-force verify, and explainable in one or two sentences
It must have no real-world interpretation and exist purely as an abstract mathematical exercise
It must use at least 50 qubits, involve cubic terms, and require a fault-tolerant quantum computer
It must be identical to the Max-Cut problem from Chapter 1, with no variation allowed
questions.explain: The lesson specifies: naturally expressible as binary decision variables with quadratic/linear cost, small enough (roughly 4-10 variables) to brute-force verify, and explainable in one or two plain-language sentences.

questions.q: For the worked Number Partitioning example with task durations d=[3,5,2,4], what are the two true optimal assignments, and what imbalance do they achieve?
options: Only x=(1,1,0,0) is optimal, achieving a 6-and-8 split
x=(0,1,1,0) and x=(1,0,0,1), both achieving a perfect 7-and-7 hour split with F(x)=0
x=(0,0,0,0) and x=(1,1,1,1), both achieving F(x)=196
There is no optimal assignment; all 16 possibilities tie
questions.explain: Brute-force checking all 16 assignments shows x=(0,1,1,0) and its mirror x=(1,0,0,1) both split the total 14 hours perfectly into 7 and 7, achieving the minimum possible F(x)=0.

questions.q: Why is Number Partitioning described as 'a well-studied special case of the QUBO family,' rather than a problem invented for teaching?
options: Because it only works for exactly 4 numbers and cannot generalize to any other count
Because Number Partitioning has never been studied before this course introduced it

Because its squared-imbalance objective expands into exactly the quadratic x_i*x_j interaction structure QUBO requires, and it is a genuinely NP-hard problem that appears in real scheduling, load-balancing, and cryptographic contexts
Because it has no connection whatsoever to the Ising model or Pauli-Z Hamiltonians
questions.explain: The squared-difference objective is already quadratic in the binary variables, converts cleanly to Ising/Pauli-Z form using the same machinery as every other problem in this course, and is a genuinely hard, widely studied problem with real applications -- not a toy invented solely for this lesson.

questions.q: What does the lesson's scoping checklist require before moving on to build the capstone workflow (Lesson 25)?
options: Access to a real quantum computer with at least 1,000 qubits
A problem with no possible classical solution method of any kind
A clearly stated objective and decision variables, an independently verifiable true optimum, and a specific classical baseline method already chosen
A guarantee that the chosen quantum method will outperform all classical alternatives
questions.explain: The checklist asks for a written objective/variables, independent verifiability of the true optimum (via brute force or similar), and a specific classical baseline already identified -- if any of these is missing, the lesson recommends scoping down further rather than proceeding.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend brute-force verification of your own capstone problem's optimum, rather than trusting whatever algorithm you test first?
options: Because brute force is required by law for any quantum computing coursework
Because brute-force verification is always faster than any other method, regardless of problem size

Because every other lesson in this course has used independent brute-force verification as the ground truth, and trusting an unverified claim risks mistaking a suboptimal or even incorrect result for the true answer
Because algorithms like QAOA and simulated annealing can never be trusted under any circumstances
questions.explain: This course has consistently used brute-force confirmation as its ground truth check (Lessons 4, 5, 20, 23, and others) -- applying that same discipline to your own capstone problem is what keeps your final comparison honest rather than assumed.
